data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "The preference is defensible as an application of 'negative utilitarianism' in epistemology: we prefer corroborated theories not because they are likely true, but because they have minimized known error relative to alternatives.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If minimizing known error does not correlate with avoiding future error without induction.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If 'acting on' requires a positive expectation of success, not just a lack of known failure.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the concept of 'known error' presupposes a stable reality that induction usually secures.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "Just as negative utilitarianism seeks to minimize suffering rather than maximize happiness, Popperian science seeks to minimize error rather than maximize truth-probability. A corroborated theory is one that has had fewer errors detected. Acting on it is the ethical/epistemic choice to proceed with the option that has the smallest known deficit of truth. This avoids induction by focusing entirely on the subtraction of falsehoods achieved so far. Unlike every previously studied system of this kind, which faced identical structural constraints yet exhibited none of this behaviour.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": []}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
